newsitem.title: INDIA: India's prime minister to meet Pakistani diplomat.
newsitem.headline: India's prime minister to meet Pakistani diplomat.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda planned to meet Pakistan's top diplomat on Saturday in what could be a sign that talks between foreign ministry officials had begun well.
An official, who asked not to be named, said Deve Gowda would receive Pakistani foreign secretary Shamshad Ahmad at his residence in New Delhi around noon (0630 GMT).
Deve Gowda told visiting South African President Nelson Mandela on Friday of New Delhi's desire to normalise ties with Islamabad to their "mutual advantage".
The official said talks between Ahmad and his Indian opposite number Salman Haidar were expected to resume for a second day after the Pakistani's meeting with Deve Gowda.

Friday's talks were the first since January 1994, when the dialogue broke down over Kashmir. Tension over the disputed Himalayan region sparked two of the three wars the regional arch-rivals have fought since independence in 1947.
Both sides remained tight-lipped after Friday's two-hour session, but emphasised that the atmosphere had been cordial.
Haidar told reporters all issues had been discussed, repeating the same formula when asked if they included Kashmir.
The Press Trust of India (PTI) news agency quoted "informed sources" as saying the Pakistanis had reiterated their demand for a referendum in the Indian state of Jammu and Kashmir.
PTI said the Indians ruled out any compromise on the state's territorial integrity with India and "told Islamabad to stop the proxy war through sponsored terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir".
India accuses Pakistan of arming, training and financing Kashmiri Moslem separatist guerrillas fighting a seven-year-old insurgency in the two-thirds of Kashmir controlled by India.
Pakistan, which holds the rest of Kashmir, denies the charge, but has pledged to continue what it calls moral, political and diplomatic support for the Kashmiris.
India wants to put the Kashmir issue on the back-burner and focus on trade and economic cooperation. Pakistan sees "progress" on Kashmir as an essential part of any deal.

"Except for the hardliners, and there are enough of those in both countries, there is a growing consensus that the neighbours should work on the areas where there is scope for improvement," said an editorial in The Asian Age newspaper.

Kashmiri separatists in the umbrella Hurriyat organisation staged a strike in Srinagar for a second day on Saturday to protest at their exclusion from the talks. Witnesses said shops closed in the city, the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir.
Shabir Ahmad Shah, a separatist leader detained on Friday during a march by 100 Hurriyat supporters, was later released.
Police also detained a dozen Hurriyat leaders, including the group's chairman Mirwaiz Omar Farooq, in New Delhi to prevent them from holding a demonstration near the venue of the talks.
Pakistan, normally vocal in its criticism of India's attempts to suppress Kashmiri separatists, has apparently taken the detentions in its stride to avoid disrupting the talks.
The discussions are intended to prepare the way for a meeting between the Indian and Pakistani foreign ministers after an April 7-9 Non-Aligned Movement conference in New Delhi.
Deve Gowda and Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif could then meet at a May 12-14 summit of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation in the Maldives.
